Chapter 3: Imperialism and the Expansion of Power Without Limits
Think back to an era when progress was measured by the size of an empire—when leaders boasted about bringing “civilization” to far-off places, and people at home imagined new horizons and untold riches just waiting to be claimed.
But if you scratch beneath that shiny surface, something deeper starts to shift. Imperialism wasn’t just about flags on maps or new markets; it changed how people thought—about power, about who belongs, and about whose lives really mattered.
In the late 1800s and early 1900s, European nations scrambled to grab as much land as they could—across Africa, Asia, and beyond. For many back home, it was a point of pride. It felt like proof their country was strong, maybe even destined for greatness.
But if you were living in those colonized places? It meant losing your land, your culture—your very sense of who you were.
Imagine a young soldier sent to a distant colony. At first, it might’ve felt like a grand adventure. But over time, reality set in. The rules everyone followed at home didn’t seem to apply anymore. Suddenly, violence and exploitation became routine. Local customs were ignored, sometimes even crushed. And a dangerous idea started to creep in: that some people simply deserved fewer rights—justified, in their minds, by racist beliefs.
Back in Europe, the changes were quieter, but just as powerful. The line between “us” and “them” got sharper. Outsiders were seen as threats, or just burdens. Even everyday language started to reflect this mindset of domination and control.
Politics wasn’t immune, either. As empires grew, governments needed new ways to keep control. Bureaucracies swelled, and the power of the state became more centralized than ever. Old checks and balances that once protected people’s freedoms? They began to fade, replaced by cold, efficient systems built to manage huge populations—sometimes by force.
For a lot of people, this was a jarring change. The sense of community that made life feel connected, even comforting, started to disappear. People were treated less like neighbors, more like cogs in a massive machine—valued only for what they could produce or contribute to the empire’s goals.
And these habits—of domination, of excluding those deemed “lesser”—they didn’t stay overseas. They came home, shaping how governments treated their own citizens. The belief that some lives matter less than others became woven into the very fabric of society.
Eventually, the limits of endless expansion became impossible to ignore. Frustration and resentment built up. All those promises of boundless growth and prosperity? They started to ring hollow. The real costs—human and moral—were laid bare for everyone to see.
In this climate of disillusionment, new ideas took root—offering simple answers to messy problems. Totalitarian movements, in particular, thrived. They promised to bring back order and restore purpose, to make sure everyone knew their place.
But underneath it all, they relied on the same logic of exclusion and control that had fueled imperialism in the first place.
For those who grew up believing in the promise of progress, this new world was a bitter letdown. Sure, the world was more connected than ever—but also more divided. The dream of a better future had been replaced by suspicion, fear, and violence.
